source.title: KineBench: Benchmarking Embodied World Models via IDM-Free Kinematic Grounding
source.authors: Ze-Yu Liu; Zhang-Zhe Zhu; Yang Zhang; Chen-You Fan; Chen-Jia Bai; Xue-Long Li

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study discusses scaling in embodied video models and reports scaling results, but measures task success rather than the held-out cross-entropy loss or compute-optimal allocation named by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports complexity-conditioned scaling of embodied video-model task success. These results do not measure language-model pretraining loss, loss extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, so they are recorded under fits_no_version rather than linked to a claim version.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes one pretrained video model (Wan2.1-1.3B) on robot tasks, varying fine-tuning steps (1.5k–15k) and trajectories (10–100). It reports only closed-loop task success, at three points per axis, with no loss measurement and no power-law fit. It cites Kaplan et al. only to contrast its results. This does not measure held-out loss scaling (V1, V2, V5), compute-optimal allocation (V3), shape effects (V4), or downstream predictability against pretraining scale or loss (V6). The finding goes under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that scaling is task-complexity-dependent and nonlinear, and that broader experiments are needed. The abstract and introduction say marginal benefits of data and compute diminish as task difficulty rises. However, Section 4.4 reports the harder task (StoreCube-v2) benefiting more from longer training. The paraphrase should note this internal inconsistency.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates embodied video-model task success rather than language-model cross-entropy scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Task complexity and training-data/training-duration settings are associated with different success-rate trends.

fits_no_version.finding: For Wan2.1-1.3B fine-tuned on ManiSkill3 tasks, aggregate success rises with steps (44.83%, 47.88%, 73.33% at 1.5k/4.5k/15k) and is flat to slightly falling across data scales 10/25/50 (53.67%, 52.00%, 51.17%). Task by task, more homogeneous data lowers OpenBoxEasy success from 100% to 83.33%, while longer training raises StoreCube-v2 from 13.34% to 69.52%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gains in embodied task success from more fine-tuning data or steps for video world models are non-monotonic and depend on task complexity.

record.problems: The scaling analysis uses one architecture (Wan2.1 1.3B), task-success rates rather than held-out loss, and limited data and training regimes. The authors call for broader experiments across architectures and data regimes. Uncertainty for the reported scaling success rates is not stated.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation of loss fits from small runs to larger runs.
Compute-optimal split between parameters and tokens.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss form in video or fine-tuning regimes. Only task success is reported, at three points, with no fit.
Downstream performance versus pretraining scale or loss. Only fine-tuning steps and data of a single model are varied.
Dependence of exponents or allocation on setup and fitting choices.

missing.what: Wan2.1-1.3B at the default 7.5k steps (43.96%) in Suite 3. This is the reference point for the step series.

record.verdict_notes: This is a benchmark paper. Its scaling analysis covers fine-tuning only, on one 1.3B model, with no uncertainty reported for the scaling numbers. It is not an original source. The sole engagement with the claim is a citation of Kaplan et al. as a contrast. The data-scale configuration labels (Scale 10/25/50) versus the text's 10–100 trajectories are not fully reconciled in the paper.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs' held-out loss from fits on small runs.
Loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute and its trend with compute.
Effects of architecture shape at fixed parameter count on language-model loss.
Whether the same power-law form holds for loss in other modalities or training regimes; this paper reports embodied-task success rates, not loss.
Predictability of downstream language-model task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted loss-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices.
